children.text: Sarah has spent a decade building large React applications at design-system scale. She teaches the fundamentals the way she wishes she had learned them — by building.
Marcus is a staff engineer focused on the hard parts of the frontend/backend boundary: caching, invalidation, and resilience under load.

title: Frontend
description: Interfaces, frameworks, and the craft of the browser.

title: Data & APIs
description: Fetching, caching, and serving data to modern apps.

title: Developer Craft
description: Testing, tooling, and habits that compound.

title: JSX Fundamentals
keyPoints: Write JSX without a cheat sheet

children.text: We start with the only JSX syntax rule that matters: it is an expression, not a string. Everything you can compute, you can render.

proTip: When in doubt, wrap your JSX thought in parentheses — it is always an expression.

resources.title: Introducing JSX
resources.description: The official React docs page this lesson expands on.

title: Components & Props
keyPoints: Split a page into a component tree
Pass props and type them in TypeScript
Know when a component is too big

children.text: Components are functions that take props and return JSX. We draw the tree first, then code it top-down.

resources.title: Exercise repo
resources.description: Starter code for the component-tree exercise.

title: State Basics
keyPoints: Use useState for simple local state
Find the right place to put state

children.text: State is data that changes over time. We build a counter, then break it and fix it to see why updates must create new values.

title: Lists & Keys
keyPoints: Choose stable keys and why index keys hurt

children.text: Keys are how React matches the old list to the new one. We demo the bugs you get when you pick them badly.
Event handlers are props too. We cover the synthetic event system and the classic onClick={doThing()} bug.
In a controlled form React owns the input value. We build one field, then generalise it.

title: Why Server State Is Different
keyPoints: Name the four states of a fetch
Why useState is the wrong tool for server data
Map cache layers in a real app

children.text: Client state you own; server state is a cache of someone else's truth. That difference drives every decision in this course.

resources.title: Deliberately declarative data fetching
resources.description: Background reading on the mental model.

title: REST vs Typed Clients
keyPoints: Compare fetch, axios, and typed codegen
Validate responses at runtime with Zod
Pick an approach per team size

children.text: We wire the same endpoint three ways and argue about the tradeoffs with receipts from each implementation.

title: Streaming Responses
keyPoints: Read a stream with the Streams API
Progressive UI states while data arrives

children.text: Streaming is not just for chatbots. We build a progressively-rendered search results panel.

title: Cache Layers
keyPoints: Identify every cache between you and origin

children.text: Browser, CDN, server, database — four caches, four failure modes. We trace a single request through all of them.
Invalidation is the part that bites at scale. We turn a messy write path into a small set of explicit rules.

title: Optimistic Updates
keyPoints: Mutate the cache before the server agrees

children.text: Optimism makes apps feel instant. It also makes failures your problem. We do both.

title: React Foundations
summary: From JSX to controlled forms — the fundamentals, the right way.
